#5919. Democrats plot massive spending spree after midterm rout — and Trump could help them pull it off

House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries addresses reporters on Capitol Hill following key Democratic victories in the 2026 midterm elections. Jeffries highlights the party's legislative agenda, promising to lower costs and protect essential programs for American families.

With a resounding Election Night victory behind them, Democrats are getting to work by plotting a massive government spending expansion paired with tax adjustments to pay for it. In this quest, they may find an unlikely ally in the White House.

Though the new crop of Democrats doesn’t take office until early next year, many are already announcing plans to aggressively increase government healthcare expenditures, cut checks directly to voters, restore housing assistance funding and pressure the federal government into repealing cuts to the bureaucracy.

Republicans, increasingly abandoning their once dogmatic opposition to increased social spending, could end up backing some of the measures Democrats seek to enact in their efforts to make life more affordable. President Donald Trump, for instance, expressed interest in cutting deals with liberal lawmakers on Election Night as it became apparent that the midterms were going to be disastrous for the GOP.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance, seen by many as the president's heir apparent, have made it clear that they do not categorically oppose the extension of Affordable Care Act subsidies, one of the marquee items on the Democratic agenda, but signaled that they would like to see increased verification requirements to crack down on alleged fraud. Both have also signaled an openness to raising taxes on high-earners to help the federal government balance its budget, though estimates regarding how much these new levies would raise generally fall short of the costs that would be incurred if Democrats succeed in actualizing their demands.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Senate Democrats are still firmly entrenched in their position that unless they get a deal on an extension to expiring Obamacare tax credits, they won't provide the votes to reopen the government. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

When approached by Fox News Digital, the White House kept the door open for compromise with the Democrats, so long as they don't go too far in their proposals.

"President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years and a stock market that has hit record-highs," White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.

"As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people," she continued.

Even with sizable Democratic majorities in the House and Senate, the party lacks the numbers necessary to override a presidential veto, meaning that liberals will need to work with either congressional Republicans or the White House if they want to enact key portions of their agenda.

"Republicans did not lose seats because of healthcare," Michael Cannon, the Cato Institute’s director of health policy studies, told Fox News Digital when asked about whether the president should compromise with Democrats by reinstating the subsidies. "Republicans did not lose seats because they let the Obamacare subsidies for the wealthy expire, because that's what those were. When we talk about enhanced subsidies, we're talking about subsidies for people making up to $600,000 per year. That's what Democrats put in place. That's what the president rightly let expire. That's not why Republicans lost seats and, so, the president should not be afraid of standing up to the industry."

TRUMP HANDING 1 MILLION AMERICANS OBAMACARE REFUND CHECKS IN 30 STATES

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., left, accompanied by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., points to a poster depicting rising medical costs if Congress allows the Affordable Care Act tax credits to expire in December as he speaks to reporters following a Democratic policy luncheon at the U.S. Capitol Building on October 15, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The massive proposed spending hikes, if they are successful, would take place as the United States’ annual deficit continues to grow, reaching nearly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, while the government faces down a looming financial disaster as Social Security's retirement trust fund approaches depletion and Congress confronts difficult choices over taxes and benefits.

Simply paying the interest on America’s debt cost the federal government over $1 trillion during the 2026 fiscal year.

Cannon argued that, if the government spends at unsustainable levels over a long enough time period, eventually bond markets will react negatively, reducing the supply of credit and forcing the government to make steep spending cuts, as has happened in Greece and under fiscally irresponsible nations. Some on the left, however, maintain that no such shock would occur as the wealthy can simply be taxed more to reduce the need for borrowing.

Though money is tight in Washington, Democrats have not pared back their spending ambitions.

The crown jewel of the Democratic spending agenda is healthcare, specifically restoring Medicaid funding and Affordable Care Act subsidies.

"During the first 100 days, House Democrats must act to reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote in a manifesto published Nov. 4.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the healthcare cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would reduce federal Medicaid spending by about $1.2 trillion between 2026 and 2035 at the cost of cutting enrollment in the program by about 13 million during that roughly 10-year period. As of publication, approximately 65.7 million people are enrolled in Medicaid.

Republicans, especially the president, may be reluctant to work with Democrats to repeal parts of the OBBA, given the sheer amount of political capital they burned to get the bill across the finish line. The extension or expansion of ACA tax credits, however, may be more fertile ground for a bipartisan agreement.

DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE

Democrats, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Chuck Schumer and Gov. Gavin Newsom, have made some unexpected alliances during President Trump's second term. (Shutterstock/AP)

Trump, for instance, said in November 2025 that he would "rather not" extend enhanced ACA tax credits, but conceded that "some kind of extension may be necessary," signaling that he is at least willing to use the subsidies as a bargaining chip during negotiations. Vance, meanwhile, has stated that the subsidies "go to some people deservedly," but argued that they lend themselves to fraud while teasing a healthcare agreement he said would please both parties.

Extending the enhanced ACA subsidies would come with a hefty price tag. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that making the expanded tax credits permanent would add roughly $350 billion to federal deficits between 2026 and 2035, while helping approximately 3.8 million more Americans obtain health insurance in 2035.

The annual impact on the federal deficit would also climb over time, from about $23 billion in 2026 to nearly $44 billion in 2035. And because CBO's estimate only covers a 10-year period, the government would face additional costs beyond that window if the subsidies remained in place.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., accompanied by House Minority Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Cali., House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., Rep. Frank Pallone Jr., D-N.J., Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Or., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., speaks following a Democratic leadership meeting at the U.S. Capitol on April 8, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Some healthcare experts argue that the federal government's spending is only part of the picture. They contend that pouring more money into insurance subsidies without addressing the underlying cost of medical care can also drive up healthcare prices, potentially leaving taxpayers and consumers paying more over time.

"If you want to know why healthcare is so expensive in the United States, why we spend more than any other country, why prices are higher, look at what Democrats are doing right now," Cannon told Fox News Digital. "Government subsidies drive up prices, they drive up healthcare spending ... the most inefficient healthcare sector in the world is using Democrats in particular, but Republicans too, I don't want to be unfair ... to get the government to keep pumping more and more money into that health sector."

Economists generally hold that subsidizing demand for a good by providing subsidies, without increasing the supply of that good, will lead to increased costs across the market. Proponents of expanded government healthcare often counter that any reductions in efficiency or increases to costs, if such things really occur, are worth enduring to ensure coverage is more equitably distributed.

Progressive Democrats led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Terri Sewell have pushed Jeffries to expand Medicare to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, set aside funds for medical debt relief and restore funding to the National Institutes of Health — proposals that could cost billions more.

Some Democratic leaders have major spending proposals extending beyond healthcare. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, seen by many as a top contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, released a policy document following Election Night outlining roughly 200 policy proposals that he would like to see from the newly elected Congress.

Among them are restoring government jobs at the Departments of Health and Human Services and Education, increased spending on infrastructure projects, pouring money into housing assistance programs and shoring up food assistance funding, among other priorities.

PROGRESSIVES WANT TO TAX BILLIONAIRES FIRST, AND YOU'RE NEXT ON THE LIST

Congressional Democrats hold a rally and press conference to announce their opposition to a Republicans plan to cut Medicaid in the Cannon House Office Building on Capitol Hill on May 13, 2025 in Washington, DC. House Republicans released a spending plan this week that would cause millions of poor Americans to lose Medicaid and millions more to pay higher fees, all part of President Donald Trump's budget priorities. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Jeffries and his congressional allies, meanwhile, also highlighted restoring SNAP funding, providing more government resources to cover childcare costs and subsidizing housing expenses. Some economists have argued that, by subsidizing demand for certain goods without stimulating increased supply, the government can inadvertently raise the cost of goods for everyone.

On the Democratic caucus's left-wing flank, independent Sen. Bernie Sanders argued that Democrats must use their resounding victory to demand a $12,000 payment to each working-class family of four, free tuition at public universities, universal free childcare, making Medicare available to 55-year-olds, increasing Social Security benefits by $2,400 a year and boosting teacher pay. While unlikely to make its way through Congress, Sanders’ agenda would cost trillions.

"The Democratic Socialists want to go much further, with universal healthcare alone, which would cost between $40 trillion and $70 trillion — roughly $300,000 to $500,000 per household," Rachel Greszler, a senior research fellow at Advancing American Freedom, a think tank affiliated with former Vice President Mike Pence, told Fox News Digital. "The entire socialist agenda calls for an estimated $71 trillion to $212 trillion in new spending over the next decade — that’s between $500,000 and $1,600,000 for every household in the US."

'SQUAD' MEMBER URGES DEMS TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF MIDTERM SWEEP BY PASSING FAR-LEFT POLICIES

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, speaks to members of the media following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Paying for all of this without running up the national debt too much is also on the minds of Democrats, and represents another area where they may find common ground with the GOP.

Sen. Ron Wyden has floated taxing the unrealized gains of some billionaires; Democratic leadership has proposed increasing the corporate income tax; many Democratic senators have argued that additional taxes should be levied against those they deem to be high earners, and some have stated that taxes should be imposed on fast-growing sectors of the economy, such as data centers.

While many of these tax hikes will likely be off the table for Republicans, Trump, Vance and a handful of congressional Republicans have expressed openness to taking more money from highly productive members of society.

Vance, per reports, indicated that he would have been open to a higher tax rate for people earning more than $1 million during internal White House discussions in 2025, though the vice president has publicly expressed skepticism that taxing wealthy Americans alone could solve the country’s fiscal problems. Trump, meanwhile, has said that he would be "OK" with taxing higher earners more to assist lower- and middle-income workers — a proposal that roughly matches the Democratic policy agenda.

Democratic Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Mark Kelly have proposed exactly that through their Working Americans' Tax Cut Act, which would cap the effective tax rate for most Americans while introducing a series of surtaxes on those making over $1 million per year. The University of Pennsylvania, home to one of the best business schools in the world, estimated that the proposal would net the federal government roughly $264 billion over a decade, which is not enough to cover the extension of ACA subsidies.

The University of Pennsylvania's model did not take into account economic feedback effects, meaning that potential lost revenue from reduced investment or work was not captured in its estimate.

Republican Sens. Bernie Moreno and Josh Hawley have backed increased taxes on high earners to pay for Social Security extensions and Child Tax Credit expansion, respectively. Rep. Andy Harris, a Republican from Maryland, has also expressed openness to a higher rate or a new bracket for million-dollar earners.

Democratic Sens. Ron Wyden and Elizabeth Warren, meanwhile, recently introduced a bill that would raise the tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4%, which analysts at the Tax Foundation and the University of Pennsylvania predict would raise either $242 billion or $300 billion, respectively, over 10 years. Combined with the millionaire tax proposal, it would generate enough revenue to offset extended ACA subsidies but would not come close to generating enough revenue to match the costs of expanding Medicaid.

U.S. DEBT BLOWS PAST $40 TRILLION, JEOPARDIZING QUALITY OF LIFE FOR EVERY AMERICAN

Housing affordability has emerged as a top political and economic issue as many Americans continue to grapple with high home prices and mortgage rates. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

Wealth tax proposals from the Democrats' left-wing flank, while projected to raise far more in revenue for the government, have proven to be politically toxic and have drawn the ire of economists for potentially crippling economic growth.

A near-term tax hike, however, may not be necessary if all the Democratic talk of healthcare funding is simply political posturing, something Cannon views as likely.

"This is all kabuki here. This is not real health reform that we're talking about. All that Democrats apparently have to offer is more spending, more spending at a time when they know that existing levels of government spending on healthcare are not popular with voters," he said, pointing to the fact that voters failed to approve a billionaire tax in California to fund state healthcare. "Democrats are offering only one idea, and they know that it won't fly, but they're going through the motions because they think they can get a political advantage by saying that Republicans don't care about people."

Lofty Democratic spending ambitions are not limited to the federal government.

With state legislatures and governors’ mansions across the country falling into Democratic hands, public expenditures are likely to boom.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, for instance, pledged on the campaign trail to tap $17 billion from the state's rainy day fund to send $1,500 checks to every Texas household, a proposal that would require legislative approval and has since been introduced in the state Senate.

While Republicans may be eager to slam Hinojosa for pulling cash from Texas’ reserves to send payments to voters, they will be forced to grapple with the fact that Trump promised to do the same, but on a much larger scale, if the GOP came out on top during the midterms.

#5918. Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: Can South Africa Tackle HIV Without the U.S.?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration took a chainsaw to global health programs, including the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has provided around $8 billion to South Africa since 2003. South Africa pays for most of its own HIV programs, including 90 percent of its antiretroviral drugs. Still, the collapse of PEPFAR was devastating, shuttering clinics for high-risk groups and leaving thousands of health workers without jobs.

South Africa is home to around 8 million people living with HIV, or around 20 percent of the global HIV population. Approximately 6 million of them are on treatment, but the country still records around 170,000 new infections each year.

When South Africa began rolling out lenacapavir this summer, the landscape had changed dramatically. U.S.-South Africa relations have deteriorated, as Trump has objected to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice and accused the country of committing genocide against white Afrikaners. Those tensions have compounded uncertainty for the HIV program.

Last year, the United States provided South Africa with $115 million to keep core HIV services running, but in June, the Trump administration said it would end all PEPFAR funding for the country in the coming months. Washington also excluded South Africa from global health financing deals struck this year with other African countries. Even as the United States supports the lenacapavir launch elsewhere, it isn’t doing so in South Africa.

In an email, a U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed that the political rift played a role in the decision to phase out PEPFAR funding. The spokesperson said PEPFAR was never meant to be a permanent initiative and that South Africa is “more than capable of supporting its own health programs” as a middle-income country.

It’s a departure from decades of U.S. foreign policy, said Jirair Ratevosian, a former senior PEPFAR official under President Joe Biden. “South Africa and the United States have never been perfectly aligned on foreign policy,” Ratevosian said. But the United States “was able to compartmentalize those disagreements and still cooperate on other big areas of interest that were aligned, and HIV was always one of those.”

Now, South Africa is left to manage its lenacapavir rollout without its historically biggest donor. It’s an early test of whether the country’s post-PEPFAR transition can become a blueprint for weathering the U.S. retreat from global health—or is a cautionary tale.

South African officials have downplayed the loss of U.S. support. In June, a health ministry spokesperson urged people not to panic, saying the government has “long been working on a self-reliance plan.” Officials have not released a formal plan, but they point to local drug manufacturing, stronger public health systems, and regional collaboration on HIV as important steps.

South Africa had a head start in this effort, as PEPFAR already accounted for less than 25 percent of the country’s HIV prevention funding, compared with around 80 percent in neighboring Mozambique and Zimbabwe, according to the Joint U.N. Program on HIV/AIDS last year.

At the launch of the lenacapavir rollout in June, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told a stadium crowd that the drug would mark a “turning point” for South Africa. Prevention remains a challenge in the country; until now PrEP has only been widely available as a daily pill, which can be difficult to access or stay on. South Africa planned to roll out a different shot that offers two months of protection last year, but high prices and PEPFAR disruptions stalled that effort.

Experts think the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot could be a game-changer. Modeling suggests that if between 1.7 million and 2.9 million South Africans get on lenacapavir each year, new infections could fall by as much as 31 percent, potentially allowing the country to eliminate HIV as a public health threat as soon as 2039. But first, South Africa must get the drug to people who need it.

In June, Ramaphosa said 3 million people will be offered lenacapavir over the next three years. The government has already secured enough doses to cover 456,000 people, funded with $29.2 million from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The first tranche was allocated to 360 public health facilities in high-burden districts, but as of mid-October, just under 79,000 South Africans had started lenacapavir, according to health ministry data.

Activists are frustrated by what they view as a sluggish rollout driven by funding gaps, insufficient planning, and regulatory bottlenecks. Some South African clinics have turned away patients seeking lenacapavir, some after running out of doses and others over logistical problems. Early in the rollout, facilities in the capital of Pretoria lacked HIV testing kits—a prerequisite to get the shot—or had not yet trained nurses to administer the drug.

“It’s a drip feed of supplies,” said Fatima Hassan, a human rights lawyer and the founder of the Health Justice Initiative in Cape Town. The U.S. funding cuts and the pace of the rollout are “putting our entire health system in jeopardy and all the gains we’ve made in the last 20 years at risk.”

The government has tried to plug some of the funding gaps left by the United States. Last year, the South African Treasury allocated around $45 million in emergency funding to cover some HIV programs, roughly one-tenth of what PEPFAR contributed in 2024. But that money does not resolve the question of what will happen to these services in the long term.

The State Department spokesperson said the United States would “reconsider future health assistance during the phase-out period”—but only if South Africa takes “concrete, demonstrable action” to remedy the Trump administration’s accusations that its government seizes land from white farmers, among other complaints.

South African Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi has said the country plans to eventually finance its lenacapavir program itself, with help from donors. “To establish a couple million doses-deep lenacapavir program in the next couple of years, we will need outside help,” said Gesine Meyer-Rath, a health economist at the University of the Witwatersrand and Boston University.

But it is not yet clear which donors will provide that help. The Global Fund, which supported the initial rollout, plans to cut South Africa’s HIV/AIDS funding by 26 percent in its next allocation cycle as it tightens its focus on the poorest countries hit hardest by HIV, TB, and malaria. A South African health ministry spokesperson did not respond to questions about the lenacapavir rollout or its “self-reliance plan.”

South Africa is betting that a generic form of lenacapavir will hit the market just as the initial supply runs out, allowing the government to roll out the drug to hundreds more clinics. Gilead Sciences, the U.S. developer of lenacapavir, agreed to make a generic version available in 120 lower- and middle-income countries, including South Africa, for $40 per person per year; it is expected by the end of the year in Zambia and elsewhere in 2027. The Global Fund negotiated a confidential price with the drugmaker for the initial shots in South Africa and other recipient countries, but brand-name lenacapavir goes for roughly $28,000 per person per year in the United States. South African health officials say the generic price must be brought down to $25 to guarantee “universal access.”

Eventually, South Africa wants to manufacture lenacapavir itself, but that effort has also encountered roadblocks. In 2024, three South African pharmaceutical companies asked Gilead for permission to make generic versions, but they were rejected because they could not handle the 28-step process of synthesizing the drug’s active ingredient. South Africa’s government is now working with Gilead and technical advisors to make local production possible.

Clinicians and civil society groups warn that supply isn’t the only problem—it’s also about getting the lenacapavir shots to those who need it most, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, and injectable drug users. But the 12 PEPFAR-funded specialized clinics and community-based outreach for these key populations, which served more than 63,000 people, have not been replaced.

“I do not think that the people who are suffering access issues because of the PEPFAR cuts are going to be the ones to get the drug,” said Kate Rees, a public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute, which suspended its PEPFAR-funded programs. “We know how to reach key populations, and waiting for them in the clinic is not it.”

Meyer-Rath, the health economist, said she has attended early planning meetings with government officials who want to reopen services for these populations and try to integrate patients into public health facilities—but that the budget available is “nonexistent or marginal.”

Another challenge: PEPFAR covered around 40 percent of South Africa’s HIV data workforce, which tracks infections and treatment uptake in HIV hot spots. With fewer of those workers, the patients who miss out on lenacapavir because they fall through the cracks of the traditional health system—as vulnerable groups tend to do—may go uncounted, making it harder to identify problems and surge support where it’s needed.

The next phase of the lenacapavir rollout is fast approaching, and it will test the country’s infrastructure as well as its supply. The first South Africans to receive the drug are due for their second shot in December, and clinics must provide an HIV test and an injection for each of them every six months going forward.

South Africa’s experience is likely to shape rollouts elsewhere, but other early adopters offer their own lessons. Kenya, which launched the drug in February, has used drop-in centers to reach key populations, though it has also struggled with shortages. Meanwhile, Zambia launched with just 500 doses in late 2025, and up to 85 percent of patients there and in Eswatini—which shares a border with South Africa—have returned on time for their second shot, according to Bhekisisa, a South African media outlet.

Lenacapavir is now being scaled up in 12 low- and middle-income countries, with 17 more countries due to receive it by early 2027, according to AVAC, an HIV prevention advocacy group. The rollout of generic lenacapavir next year will be another turning point. It’s a reminder that even if South Africa sticks the landing, there’s still a long way to go to defeat HIV.

“Right now, we are wobbling a bit, and the world is watching us wobble,” Meyer-Rath said. “But basically, it’s either the [South African] government or it’s not. No one will fund the system. We have to.”

Gabriela Galvin is an award-winning freelance journalist in London. She covers health and social policy.

#5916. Inside the Denver gathering where Democrats’ upbeat, Obama-era feel meets the 2028 race

DENVER — Live music, concert-style campaign posters and a packed schedule of Democratic leaders set the scene in Denver, where party strategists and potential 2028 contenders gathered to celebrate midterm gains and start shaping what comes next.

The industrial-style venue, with indoor and outdoor spaces, gave the two-day "What’s Next" gathering a festival feel. Democrats moved between political programming, live music and social events.

Beneath the party atmosphere, potential contenders tested their messages and sized up the field, as Democrats began jockeying over the party’s direction and who might lead it in 2028.

The event had an unmistakably Obama-era feel, with its hopeful message and celebratory campaign atmosphere.

DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE

Concert-style campaign posters at Denver’s Mission Ballroom set the scene for the "What’s Next" gathering and gave it an Obama-era campaign feel on Nov. 12, 2026. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

Matt Corridoni, a Democratic strategist and communications adviser at Majority Democrats, said the comparison made sense.

"The theme of that campaign was hope, and a lot of folks who are here now either worked on that campaign or were inspired by that campaign," Corridoni said. "I think one of the themes of this event is hopefulness for the Democratic Party moving forward. It’s a comparison that doesn’t shock me."

That hopeful energy showed up in the event’s posters and playful swag, some of which Ahmad Ali, communications director for the Searchlight Institute, helped design.

DEMOCRATS RIDE MIDTERM WAVE AS 2028 HOPEFULS GATHER IN DENVER TO MAP THEIR NEXT MOVES

Baseball hats and shirts at the "What’s Next" gathering in Denver featured slogans including "new deal democrat," "tax-and-spend liberal" and "Our Get Along Shirt." (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

"I think we’re seeing a Democratic Party that is younger, brighter and way more emboldened to achieve what it wants to," Ali told Fox News Digital. "So this conference, its aesthetics, whether it’s the posters you see, the fun hats, all that — it just speaks to the confidence of the era."

Ali said the party’s energy could signal a break from what he described as a period of political stagnation, with voters looking for new choices in 2028.

He pointed to former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign and President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory as moments that captured the political mood, while arguing that the Biden era did not carry the same cultural force.

Attendees gather outside Denver’s Mission Ballroom during the "What’s Next" conference, where Democrats discussed the party’s direction and the 2028 race on Nov. 12, 2026. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

"We are at the end of the Trump era, but we’re also at the end of whatever the sort of period of stuckness has plagued the Democratic Party," Ali said. "And I think that is very important, not just for Democrats, but also for all voters, because now maybe they’re going to have better options come 2028."

The gathering offered a first glimpse of how Democrats hope to turn their midterm momentum into a path to 2028.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#5914. La última oportunidad para la paz

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.

En algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable. Las guerras de agresión, como las de Ucrania, el Líbano o Irán, aumentan y siembran horror, ruina y el temor a una confrontación global. Los gobiernos piensan cada vez más en la guerra como algo para lo que hay que prepararse y presupuestar. El gasto militar no deja de crecer, las carreras tecnológicas y armamentísticas se intensifican, y cada vez más países se plantean si deberían dotarse de un arsenal nuclear disuasorio que garantice su seguridad.

No hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra. Supone regresar a una norma que imperó durante la mayor parte de la historia de la humanidad. La guerra era el eje vertebrador del sistema internacional. Era la vía natural por la que los Estados zanjaban sus disputas o ensanchaban su territorio a costa de vecinos más débiles.

Pero la inmensa devastación que produjeron las dos guerras mundiales en la primera mitad del siglo XX hizo inaceptable ese statu quo. Los países se unieron en un empeño común: que la guerra dejara de ser un instrumento legítimo de la política de Estado y pasara a ser un acto ilegal. Las guerras no terminaron en 1945, pero durante años la comunidad internacional las condenó de forma abrumadora.

En las últimas décadas, sin embargo, el compromiso de los gobiernos con la causa de la paz se ha debilitado. En 2003, millones de personas salieron a las calles en cientos de ciudades para oponerse a la invasión de Irak liderada por Estados Unidos. Y, aun así, la guerra siguió adelante. Iniciada a partir de premisas falsas y en violación del derecho internacional, arrasó Irak, agravó la inestabilidad regional y avivó el resentimiento y el terrorismo contra los países occidentales. Aquel conflicto marcó, además, un punto de inflexión. Desde entonces, la búsqueda de la paz ha ido retrocediendo en la agenda internacional, arrinconada por la creciente competencia geopolítica y la desatención o la indiferencia hacia los esfuerzos multilaterales que durante décadas pusieron freno a la guerra.

Este camino conduce a una nueva guerra mundial: la catástrofe que el orden del siglo XX se propuso evitar. Ante ese futuro sombrío en el horizonte, los gobiernos deben reaprender el arte de oponerse a la guerra. Todos los países, incluido el mío, España, tienen la responsabilidad de actuar para limitar la capacidad de otros de librar la guerra y para fortalecer las instituciones internacionales que han de ser garantes de la paz.

El éxito de este proyecto dependerá de un multilateralismo expansivo, al que yo llamo «maxilateralismo»: una cooperación que abarque al mayor número posible de países, en lugar de limitarse a pequeñas coaliciones ad hoc. Su ambición es que la guerra resulte cada vez más inviable, incluso inimaginable. En 2003, manifestantes por toda España coreaban «¡No a la guerra!». En 2026, el mundo no puede volver a ignorarlos.

Los esfuerzos internacionales por desterrar la guerra como instrumento de política nacional se remontan al Pacto Briand-Kellogg de 1928, un tratado firmado en París por 15 países, al que posteriormente se sumaron decenas más. No bastó para impedir la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero plantó una semilla. Cuando representantes de 50 países se reunieron en San Francisco en 1945 para crear las Naciones Unidas, recuperaron el espíritu y los principios del Pacto y añadieron lo que había faltado: estructura institucional. La Carta de Naciones Unidas prohibió recurrir a la amenaza o al uso de la fuerza contra la integridad territorial o la independencia política de otro Estado. Y, a diferencia de su predecesor de 1928, respaldó esa prohibición con instituciones facultadas para hacerla cumplir.

En las décadas siguientes, estas instituciones levantaron un orden que castigaba las violaciones al derecho internacional e incentivaba la cooperación y la diplomacia. Al mismo tiempo, el rechazo popular a la guerra y al militarismo de la Guerra Fría cobraba fuerza en todo el mundo. Se hizo visible en la resistencia a la guerra de Vietnam y en los movimientos de masas contra las armas nucleares. El pacifismo alcanzó su punto álgido en los años noventa, cuando una sociedad civil global pujante se movilizó en defensa de causas humanitarias y Naciones Unidas tenía autoridad para abanderar una ambiciosa agenda de paz.

Hoy, sin embargo, hay más conflictos armados que en ningún otro momento desde 1946. Según el Programa de Datos sobre Conflictos de Uppsala, en 2025 hubo 65 conflictos activos con participación estatal, el doble que en 2010. Se calcula que en estos conflictos murieron 250.000 personas: la cifra anual más alta desde el genocidio de Ruanda hace más de 30 años. Cerca de 120 millones de personas en todo el mundo siguen desplazadas por la guerra.

Y lo más inquietante: las guerras de agresión, que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas, están de vuelta. Rusia invadió Ucrania. Estados Unidos e Israel atacaron Irán. Y mientras los combates se prolongan año tras año en lugares como el Líbano, Sudán o Yemen, resulta evidente que la guerra está siendo aceptada de nuevo como algo normal.

Nada indica que esta tendencia vaya a frenarse. Los presupuestos militares se han disparado hasta niveles no vistos en generaciones, en detrimento del gasto social y de desarrollo. Solo en la última década, el gasto mundial en defensa ha aumentado más de un 40 %, y muchos países han duplicado sus presupuestos militares. Los casi 3 billones de dólares que el mundo destina cada año a defensa se acercan al producto interior bruto de todo el continente africano. Incluso países con una larga tradición de contención militar, como Alemania, Dinamarca, Japón y Noruega, se están rearmando a toda velocidad, y algunos están recuperando el servicio militar.

Aún más estremecedor es el regreso de la amenaza de guerra nuclear. Los nueve Estados con armas nucleares están modernizando sus arsenales y aumentando su capacidad destructiva. Se calcula que el arsenal de China ha pasado de entre unas 200-300 cabezas nucleares a finales de la década de 2010 a 620 este año. Corea del Norte también ha ampliado el suyo, de entre 10-20 cabezas estimadas en 2018 a unas 60 este año, y ha desarrollado plataformas de lanzamiento cada vez más sofisticadas. En marzo, Francia anunció el primer aumento de su número de cabezas nucleares desde 1992. Estados Unidos y Rusia, las dos mayores potencias nucleares del mundo, no han sido capaces de preservar el último tratado que ponía límites a sus arsenales estratégicos. Y cada vez más potencias no nucleares han empezado a plantearse adquirir armas nucleares propias.

Al mismo tiempo, la inteligencia artificial (IA) está dotando a la guerra de armas cada vez más peligrosas. La supervisión humana se reduce progresivamente a medida que la IA permite automatizar ciberataques contra redes eléctricas, hospitales y sistemas financieros. Hay sistemas de IA que ya han logrado infiltrarse en organismos públicos y han hecho posible la producción masiva de deepfakes y de campañas de desinformación.

La integración de la IA en las tecnologías nucleares es una amenaza existencial: al acelerar la toma de decisiones, comprime el tiempo disponible para el juicio humano. Del mismo modo, el uso de la IA en biotecnología podría rebajar drásticamente las barreras a la experimentación nociva y al desarrollo de armas biológicas. En ambos terrenos, esta tecnología está elevando a niveles sin precedentes el riesgo de errores de cálculo, de escaladas involuntarias y de destrucción masiva.

En conjunto, estas dinámicas multiplican las probabilidades de que cualquier crisis desemboque rápidamente en la aniquilación del planeta. Por desgracia, los países están fabricando los instrumentos de la catástrofe a la velocidad vertiginosa de la innovación, mientras que los instrumentos de control avanzan al ritmo, mucho más lento, de la diplomacia.

Los cambios políticos están alejando al mundo de la paz. Lo empujan hacia la militarización y la confrontación. Un mundo multipolar no es, por definición, más peligroso. Pero la erosión de las normas y de las instituciones que deberían encauzar las tensiones entre los distintos polos está provocando que el mundo se vuelva especialmente volátil. La competencia entre grandes potencias se intensifica: las ansias de hegemonía alientan políticas exteriores agresivas y los Estados revisionistas desafían las normas y las fronteras establecidas. El nacionalismo beligerante crece. Los movimientos de extrema derecha promueven una visión del mundo en la que las relaciones internacionales son un juego de suma cero y los países deben competir en lugar de cooperar. Incluso dirigentes de centro están adoptando la retórica de la guerra. Aunque no pretendan iniciar una, sus palabras abonan una mentalidad militarista peligrosa.

En este clima de rivalidad, las guerras de agresión se envuelven en discursos de necesidad, liberación, legítima defensa o justicia histórica. Los agresores presentan sus operaciones como inevitables, después de haber demonizado a sus adversarios para justificar un ataque preventivo. Venden cada guerra como la respuesta a la inseguridad: la guerra que acabará con todas las guerras.

Pero estas guerras no harán del mundo un lugar más seguro. Cada vez que un Estado desata una guerra de agresión, erosiona las normas que protegen a todos los países frente al uso arbitrario de la fuerza, incluido el propio Estado agresor.

Las guerras tienen un coste inmenso. Destrozan sociedades y truncan vidas. En 2025, según los registros de Naciones Unidas, al menos un civil murió en conflicto armado cada 14 minutos, y más de cinco millones de personas se vieron obligadas a huir de sus países. El coste económico también es altísimo. La guerra que enfrenta a Estados Unidos e Israel con Irán ha alterado gravemente el comercio marítimo y el tráfico aéreo y ha disparado los precios de la energía, los fertilizantes y otras materias primas. Millones de personas en todo el mundo están sufriendo las consecuencias.

La guerra genera, además, nuevos peligros. Una vez que empiezan los combates, su rumbo es imprevisible. Los conflictos tienden a arrastrar a nuevos actores y a desbordarse hacia los países vecinos. La guerra de Irán vuelve a ser un ejemplo claro. Desde febrero de 2026, Irán ha atacado objetivos en varios países del Golfo y de su entorno, acciones que España ha condenado sin excepción. Los ataques contra buques civiles y mercantes amenazan la estabilidad del conjunto de la región. Y la guerra ha reavivado los conflictos de Irak, el Líbano y Yemen.

Por último, las guerras rara vez traen una paz duradera. Al contrario: ahondan los agravios y enquistan las divisiones que alimentan la violencia del mañana. La guerra de Rusia en Ucrania, por ejemplo, ha dinamitado la confianza en Moscú. El genocidio en Gaza ha exacerbado la indignación contra Israel, y eso podría desembocar en nuevas oleadas de terrorismo. Y la guerra contra Irán ha desestabilizado aún más la región y ha lastrado la cooperación entre sus países.

El mundo tiene la responsabilidad de resistirse a la normalización de la guerra. Callar es un acto de cobardía y de complicidad. La sociedad española está dejando clara su posición: tres de cada cuatro españoles señalan la guerra como su mayor temor. Y un número aún mayor cree que se cierne otra guerra mundial.

Pero no basta con condenar la guerra en abstracto. La ambición de acabar con ella debe ir acompañada de acciones concretas que hagan cada vez más difícil que los países inicien, sostengan y justifiquen un conflicto armado.

España ha procurado actuar en esa dirección. Ha defendido las normas internacionales que marcan la diferencia entre un orden basado en reglas y otro gobernado por la fuerza. Y ha denunciado siempre los ataques armados que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas.

Desde el primer día de la guerra en Gaza, España ha reclamado un alto el fuego inmediato y permanente, la liberación de todos los rehenes y la entrada sin restricciones de la ayuda humanitaria. En mayo de 2024, España reconoció el Estado de Palestina con la esperanza de que este paso contribuyera a avanzar hacia una solución negociada y duradera del conflicto. Y ha apoyado activamente los esfuerzos de la Corte Internacional de Justicia y de la Corte Penal Internacional para que los dirigentes israelíes rindan cuentas por sus violaciones del derecho internacional humanitario. Israel tenía derecho a la legítima defensa tras los atentados terroristas del 7 de octubre. Pero ese derecho no justifica el genocidio en Gaza ni la expansión de la ocupación ilegal de Cisjordania.

Disuadir la guerra exige también elevar el coste de la agresión. El resto del mundo debe asegurarse de que quien elija hacer la guerra no pueda hacerlo sin pagar un precio. A lo largo de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, la Unión Europea ha aprobado sucesivas rondas de sanciones contra Rusia que España ha respaldado sin titubeos. España también ha prestado a Ucrania ayuda financiera, humanitaria y militar para que pueda defender su territorio y negarle a Rusia el botín de guerra.

Los países deben negarse a ayudar a las partes a extender los conflictos en curso. España, por ejemplo, mantiene un embargo de armas a Israel desde 2023. Este año, además, negó a Estados Unidos el uso de su territorio y de sus instalaciones para la guerra contra Irán. La decisión de España no fue un acto de hostilidad hacia un aliado. Tampoco fue una expresión de neutralidad ni de simpatía hacia el régimen iraní. Fue el fruto de una valoración estratégica: implicarse habría favorecido la escalada del conflicto y agravado la inseguridad regional y mundial. Para ser fiel a su compromiso con la paz, España tenía que estar dispuesta a decir no, aunque eso tuviera un coste político. Si más países hubieran actuado igual, las guerras de Gaza y de Irán habrían sido mucho más difíciles y costosas de librar.

Invertir en prosperidad es igualmente esencial. La seguridad crece cuando las sociedades son resilientes, las desigualdades se reducen y la ciudadanía puede confiar en las instituciones públicas. La decisión de España, el año pasado, de no asumir el objetivo de gasto en defensa del 5 % del PIB propuesto por la OTAN refleja esta visión. No nace de una falta de compromiso con la defensa europea. De hecho, mi Gobierno ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea, triplicando el gasto neto en defensa en los ocho años que llevo en el cargo. Pero la disuasión militar y el bienestar social deben reforzarse mutuamente. Al mantener un gasto en defensa proporcionado, España ha conservado el margen fiscal necesario para invertir 145.000 millones de euros adicionales en protección social, vivienda, sanidad y educación, y más de 30.000 millones en la transición ecológica. Son políticas que cohesionan la sociedad y, por tanto, la hacen más segura.

Los esfuerzos de un solo país tienen, sin embargo, un alcance limitado. Cortarle el oxígeno a la guerra exige la implicación de todos: un esfuerzo colectivo basado en un multilateralismo genuino. Esta es la única estrategia que ha funcionado en el pasado. El sistema multilateral construido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial abarcaba todo el planeta y contribuyó a preservar la paz entre las grandes potencias y a evitar una tercera guerra mundial.

Reforzarlo no será tarea fácil. La pugna geopolítica y una desconfianza generalizada han debilitado a Naciones Unidas, los organismos financieros internacionales, las organizaciones regionales y otras instituciones multilaterales. Muchos países las perciben como ineficaces y atrapadas en una crisis perpetua, de modo que están recurriendo a marcos alternativos para intentar poner fin a las guerras.

Algunos han optado por enfoques unilaterales, persiguiendo acuerdos transaccionales que acaban beneficiando a élites económicas y políticas y dejan al margen a las poblaciones afectadas por el conflicto. Los altos el fuego o los acuerdos de paz que logran pueden ser preferibles a la continuación de la guerra, pero cualquier paz impuesta por la ley del más fuerte, y no por el derecho, se asienta sobre cimientos frágiles.

Otros países, frustrados con el multilateralismo, han intentado formar «coaliciones de voluntarios» u otros grupos «minilaterales» para garantizar su seguridad o alcanzar acuerdos ad hoc en materia de comercio o tecnología. Este enfoque puede ser una solución temporal a la parálisis de las instituciones tradicionales, pero su carácter excluyente fragmenta aún más un orden internacional ya dividido. Lo que necesitamos no es minilateralismo, sino maxilateralismo. La cooperación internacional alcanza su verdadera fuerza cuando es—o aspira a ser—universal. Dejar a una parte del mundo fuera de estos esfuerzos es, además, incubar la confrontación de mañana.

El sistema internacional del siglo XX no era perfecto. Sus normas se han aplicado de manera desigual, sus principios se han defendido de forma inconsistente y sus procedimientos han sido desesperantemente lentos. Pero es innegable que, sin él, el mundo sería un polvorín aún mayor. Basta un ejemplo: fue una red de tratados internacionales—entre ellos, el Tratado sobre la No Proliferación de las Armas Nucleares, el Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio y el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de los Ensayos Nucleares—la que puso fin a una carrera armamentística desbocada y extraordinariamente costosa que estaba llevando al mundo al borde de una guerra nuclear.

Toda esta arquitectura institucional se está resquebrajando. Y sin ella, aspirar a preservar la paz es una quimera.

Fortalecer las instituciones multilaterales debe ser el eje central de una campaña global para relegar la guerra a los libros de historia. Para ello será necesario acometer reformas de calado que les devuelvan la legitimidad y refuercen su capacidad de actuación, dando prioridad a las medidas que más contribuyan a la paz y la seguridad.

La primera pasa por aumentar la representación en las Naciones Unidas y las instituciones de Bretton Woods. Actualizar la estructura del Consejo de Seguridad de Naciones Unidas es especialmente importante, dada su responsabilidad principal de mantener la paz internacional. Un Consejo de Seguridad con asientos permanentes y derecho de veto para las cinco potencias vencedoras de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, que en conjunto suman apenas una cuarta parte de la población mundial, no refleja el mundo de hoy. Debe ampliarse el número de miembros electos del Consejo y alargar su mandato más allá de los dos años actuales. Los nuevos asientos deben otorgarse principalmente a países de regiones infrarrepresentadas, en particular África y América Latina. Organizaciones regionales como la Unión Europea y la Unión Africana también deberían estar representadas en el Consejo, posiblemente ocupando puestos que hoy corresponden a Estados. Un Consejo de Seguridad más representativo no solo sería más justo, sino también más eficaz. Los países defienden y hacen cumplir con más empeño las normas internacionales cuando se sienten autores de ellas.

También hay que restringir estrictamente el poder de veto de los miembros permanentes, en especial cuando el Consejo de Seguridad delibere sobre casos de atrocidades masivas, genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y crímenes de guerra. En última instancia, el veto debe abolirse por completo. Solo entonces podrá el Consejo responder a todos los actos de agresión sin quedar secuestrado por las objeciones de un solo Estado.

Un espíritu similar debería orientar la transformación estructural de las instituciones financieras internacionales, en particular el Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. La distribución del poder de voto en ambas sigue reflejando los equilibrios económicos del siglo XX y, por convención, un europeo está siempre al frente del FMI y un estadounidense, del Banco Mundial. Esto debe terminar. Las economías emergentes necesitan una representación más adecuada, y los puestos de liderazgo deben estar abiertos a todos los candidatos, sea cual sea su nacionalidad. También deberán evolucionar las responsabilidades que asumen en instituciones como la Organización Mundial del Comercio los países antes considerados «en desarrollo», a medida que crecen y se incorporan al grupo de las economías más ricas. Una gobernanza económica más justa aliviaría la desigualdad y el resentimiento que con tanta frecuencia atizan la inestabilidad y los conflictos.

Otra reforma esencial consiste en revitalizar el marco internacional que contiene el riesgo de escalada nuclear. Parte de ese trabajo depende de las potencias nucleares. Corresponde a Estados Unidos y a Rusia negociar un tratado que suceda al acuerdo bilateral Nuevo START y que preserve topes verificables al despliegue de armas nucleares. Y, esta vez, China debería participar en las conversaciones.

Pero el esfuerzo más amplio exige el compromiso de todos los países. Entre sus prioridades deben figurar la ratificación del Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares, para impedir que se reanuden las pruebas nucleares, y el avance de las negociaciones sobre un Tratado de Prohibición de la Producción de Material Fisionable, que prohibiría la producción de uranio altamente enriquecido y plutonio para armas nucleares. Todos deben también trabajar conjuntamente para regular el uso de la IA en el ámbito militar, especialmente en lo que respecta a las armas nucleares, a fin de preservar el control humano sobre las decisiones de lanzamiento y minimizar el riesgo de errores fatales. Los países no nucleares deben comprometerse a no adquirir armas nucleares y deben emplear todos los medios a su alcance para instar a las potencias nucleares a reducir sus arsenales, reforzar los mecanismos de verificación y reconstruir las salvaguardas diplomáticas que durante décadas han ayudado a evitar una catástrofe nuclear.

La tecnología puede contribuir en parte a esta tarea. Los avances en imágenes por satélite, sensores remotos y análisis de datos pueden aumentar la transparencia y la supervisión del cumplimiento de los acuerdos de control de armamentos. Pero también hay que hacer mucho más para evitar situaciones que puedan precipitar una guerra. Si los Estados con armas nucleares acuerdan reducir su disponibilidad operacional y reforzar la comunicación en momentos de tensión, los gobiernos contarán con más tiempo y más medios para desactivar las crisis. Cada país debe proteger sus sistemas de mando y control frente a los ciberataques y la manipulación informativa impulsada por la IA, de modo que una falsa alarma o un error de cálculo no desencadenen jamás una guerra nuclear.

Por último, es prioritario trabajar para garantizar que el sistema de justicia internacional pueda hacer cumplir las decisiones de los tribunales. Desmantelar la Corte Penal Internacional, como pretenden algunos países, solo aseguraría la impunidad de los crímenes más atroces. La CPI no solo debe investigar y juzgar los casos de genocidio, agresión, crímenes de guerra y crímenes de lesa humanidad, sino también contar con la autoridad necesaria para llevar ante la justicia a los responsables de esos crímenes. Cuando un Estado pasa a ser parte del Estatuto de Roma, el tratado que creó la CPI, acepta someterse a la jurisdicción de la Corte. Sin embargo, si ese Estado se niega a cooperar o a entregar a un sospechoso, no existe una sanción efectiva, sino apenas una llamada de atención. Esto debe cambiar. Los Estados que den cobijo a personas imputadas por la CPI deben afrontar consecuencias legales, diplomáticas y financieras. Iniciar y librar una guerra debe tener un coste real.

La reforma de las instituciones internacionales lleva años estancada, pero la próxima elección para la Secretaría General de Naciones Unidas ofrece una ocasión excepcional para darle un nuevo impulso. Que Naciones Unidas nombrara a su primera secretaria general sería un poderoso símbolo de renovación, inclusión y adaptación institucional. La organización no puede afirmar verdaderamente que habla en nombre de toda la humanidad mientras no la haya dirigido una mujer. Alcanzar este hito podría despertar una nueva ambición y reforzar la confianza en la capacidad de las instituciones internacionales para reformarse y para que recuperen su papel a la hora de poner freno a la guerra.

Frenar la deriva del mundo hacia la guerra exigirá el compromiso más amplio posible. Ningún país, grande o pequeño, puede mirar hacia otro lado ni sumarse a las acciones que aviven la escalada. Todos debemos defender las normas internacionales que hoy ponen coto a la guerra y reformar y dotar de poder a las instituciones que mañana la harán imposible.

En última instancia, lo que hará inimaginable la guerra es una agenda de paz positiva que aborde las causas profundas de la inseguridad. Cada paso hacia la erradicación de la pobreza, la ampliación del acceso a una educación de calidad, el avance de la igualdad de género, el fortalecimiento de las instituciones democráticas y el aumento de la resiliencia ante los desastres naturales atenúa también las condiciones que engendran la violencia.

Las instituciones financieras internacionales deben ser capaces de proporcionar financiación con rapidez, a gran escala y a un coste razonable, para que ningún país en desarrollo se vea obligado a elegir entre atender su deuda e invertir en su población. Los bancos multilaterales de desarrollo deben poder movilizar fondos para las transiciones ecológica y digital, de modo que las migraciones climáticas y la disputa por los recursos no se conviertan en detonantes de conflictos entre Estados. Y el Acuerdo sobre Pandemias de la Organización Mundial de la Salud debe ultimarse y entrar en vigor para garantizar que todos los países puedan acceder a vacunas y tratamientos cuando llegue la próxima emergencia sanitaria mundial.

Por eso España ha procurado situar el desarrollo en el centro de su política exterior. El Gobierno español ha sido un firme defensor de los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible de la ONU para 2030 y, el año pasado, la ciudad de Sevilla acogió la Cuarta Conferencia Internacional sobre la Financiación para el Desarrollo, donde la comunidad internacional se comprometió a aligerar la carga de la deuda de los países vulnerables y a desbloquear inversiones para el desarrollo sostenible. España también ha promovido iniciativas como el Centro Global para Canjes de Deuda por Desarrollo, lanzado junto con el Banco Mundial; la Alianza multilateral por las Cláusulas de Suspensión de Deuda, que permite a los países vulnerables suspender el pago de su deuda tras una catástrofe; y un mecanismo propio para ofrecer hasta 60 millones de euros anuales en alivio de deuda a países en desarrollo. Además, España ha respaldado, junto con instituciones multilaterales y organizaciones internacionales, iniciativas de financiación climática, salud global, igualdad de género, seguridad alimentaria y protección social. Estas políticas de desarrollo son también políticas de construcción de paz.

Un proyecto ambicioso de movilización global en favor del derecho internacional y de un multilateralismo genuino puede parecer poco realista. Pero ya hemos visto lo que ocurre cuando la normalización de la guerra arrastra a la humanidad al infierno. Los hombres y las mujeres que se levantaron de entre las ruinas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el capítulo más oscuro de nuestra historia, encontraron la manera de construir un orden mundial multilateral. La pregunta a la que se enfrenta nuestra generación es si seremos capaces de preservar el imperio de la ley o permitiremos el regreso de la ley de la jungla. Si construiremos el mundo del mañana con visión de futuro y cooperación, o a través del caos y del dolor de otra guerra mundial. Debemos elegir bien mientras la decisión siga estando en nuestras manos.

#5913. Democrats Can’t Return to Pre-Trump Foreign Policy

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Democrats Can’t Return to Pre-Trump Foreign Policy

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

The impulse to reverse course on Trump’s alliance policy is understandable. The president has brought two years of vitriol and abuse upon the United States’ closest friends—from a trade war with Canada to threats to invade Greenland—with clear strategic costs. But the flaws of his approach, and its broad unpopularity with the American public, are not a mandate for reflexive reversal. Nevertheless, there is a growing view in both Washington and allied capitals that, under new congressional leadership and with a new administration just two years away, Washington should take a maximally conciliatory approach to its friends. Apology tours, day-one tariff repeals, and the reinstatement of withdrawn troops in allied countries are all cited as necessary steps to regain lost trust.

The problem with that approach is twofold. First, it prioritizes rebuilding trust with allies over something more important—transforming old alliance bargains. The U.S. alliance system was built for the early Cold War world and used conventional and nuclear deterrence to keep threats far from the country’s shores. Its record of success is remarkable: No U.S. ally has ever been attacked, and U.S. treaty guarantees were invoked just once—on Washington’s behalf following the Sept. 11 attacks. But in the post-Cold War world, the United States and its allies need to cooperate on artificial intelligence, securing vital supply chains, aligning on climate and industrial policy, and combatting threats in cyberspace. Reembracing alliances without insisting on much-needed modernization would miss the chance to update them for new opportunities and threats, leaving the U.S. alliance network far less effective.

Reflexive policy reversal also ignores the ways in which allies approach the United States differently after Trump’s reelection and punitive second term. U.S. leadership on global issues is now constrained by a four-year problem. Having seen the United States succumb to political chaos twice in a decade at the expense of its own global position, friends and partners around the world will assume that any future deal they cut with the United States is only good for four years, until power changes hands again. If the United States wants close cooperation from allies in this world, then it will have to give them some space to build autonomy and resilience in case Washington defects again.

Taking this advice would prompt Democratic leaders to resist conventional wisdom on two issues in particular: tariffs and defense burden-sharing.

Trump’s trade war has proven to be both bad policy and bad politics, and it has hit U.S. allies as hard as its competitors. Many allies will argue that tariff reversals are an essential precondition for earning back their trust in the post-Trump era. But pursuing a unilateral, blanket repeal of tariffs on allies and partners—whether as an act of Congress or in the early days of a new administration—would be a mistake. Instead, Democrats can use their newfound control of Congress to check illegal tariffs that have driven up costs for American consumers, such as tariffs on forced labor, and repeal senseless duties on Canada. Such steps should pave the way for a broader international-economic agenda in 2029 that strengthens the U.S. economy and restores predictability for workers and businesses. That could start with plans to lower remaining tariffs on allies as part of a new economic bargain that includes bold, joint action against unfair Chinese trade practices and new agreements on technology and supply chain cooperation. Trump’s wanton tariff leverage should be parlayed into new cooperation, rather than freely ceded, to serve the bottom line of the American people and those in friendly nations.

A phased plan for tariffs also points the way for Democrats to take a new approach to allied burden-sharing on security and defense. Denouncing Trump’s abusive approach, elevating alliances as a strategic priority, and unambiguously acknowledging China and Russia as shared threats can begin to improve U.S. relationships. But congressional Democrats should not launch an apology tour or provide slavish reassurances that undercut the progress that allies have made toward better defending themselves. Instead, Democrats should encourage allies to continue investing in their own defense in Europe and Asia, and adjust U.S. policies to actively support these efforts, even if the United States loses some influence as allies take on a greater role. Following a disastrous war with Iran that has cratered U.S. defense stockpiles, Congress should fund super-charged efforts to coproduce munitions and other critical systems alongside allies to rebuild deterrence. And, notwithstanding the flawed process by which the Trump administration has approached its ongoing global force posture review, Democrats should bring an open mind to the strategic benefits of a rebalanced U.S. presence in some regions.

Newly empowered, Democrats should seize the opportunity to reassert allies as central to U.S. global strategy. But that should not mean a return to old patterns of burden-sharing, which too often let allies off the hook and created dependencies that they will no longer accept and the United States should not encourage. Nor should Washington fall back on traditional modes of collaboration, which privileged military commitments whose benefits may feel abstract and undervalued the economic and technological domains that most benefit Americans. The Trump shock to the U.S. alliance system has come with high costs, and most of this approach should be rejected. But Democrats should also identify where policies of the past two years have created new openings or new leverage and use those opportunities wisely, rather than giving them away for free. Rebuilding critical U.S. relationships is essential, but it is a long-term project. After two Trump presidencies, quick policy concessions will not overcome the structural sources of allied skepticism about U.S. reliability.

The world that the next U.S. president meets in 2029 will look dramatically different than the one of 2025 or 2021. The post-Cold War era has ended in a convulsion, and the Trump presidency, which has intentionally ravaged the United States’ global role, has two years of chaos remaining. Rather than attempt to run down the clock through 2028 and overturn his disastrous policies wholesale, congressional Democrats have a chance to build a policy bridge to a new era. By prioritizing the renovation and resilience in the U.S. global alliance system, Congress can work with—rather than in reflexive opposition to—the epochal global shifts that have taken place and position Washington to inaugurate a new era of global leadership in 2029.

Rebecca Lissner is a senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as a deputy assistant to the president and principal deputy national security advisor to the vice president in the Biden-Harris administration. X: @RebeccaLissner

Mira Rapp-Hooper is a partner at the Asia Group and a visiting senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was the senior director for East Asia and Oceania at the White House’s National Security Council from 2023-2025.
